frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over Sonatrach and pipeline exports, but European buyers are pushing for more flexible terms and alternative suppliers. Infrastructure investment remains constrained by state-led regulation and price sensitivity.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese and Gulf infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign contractors are active in ports, construction, and industrial projects, but Algiers generally preserves ownership and strategic control over critical assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign oil-sector dominance
frictionVectors.details: Angola has improved regulatory oversight, but offshore production and technology remain heavily dependent on international energy companies and external financing. Declining output heightens pressure to attract capital on less favorable terms.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor geopolitics
frictionVectors.details: The corridor increases Angola's strategic value for copper and cobalt exports from the DRC and Zambia. Its development brings Western and Gulf interest while raising concerns over external influence and unequal value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port of Cotonou dependency
frictionVectors.details: Benin is strengthening Cotonou as a regional logistics hub, but trade flows remain vulnerable to Nigerian policy shifts and foreign-backed infrastructure financing. Strategic autonomy is limited by dependence on imported fuel and external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity spreading south from the Sahel threatens transport routes and investment in northern areas. Security cooperation with regional and external partners is expanding, but it may increase operational dependence.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has used its diamond position to secure a larger share of value and greater marketing influence. The main risk is weaker global diamond demand and continued reliance on a narrow export base.

frictionVectors.title: New minerals and external capital
frictionVectors.details: Copper, nickel, and other mineral projects could diversify exports, but their development will depend on foreign technology, financing, and regional transport infrastructure. Gaborone retains comparatively strong institutional leverage over concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector state consolidation
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater control over gold production, licensing, and refining while reducing the role of Western firms. Limited technical capacity and insecurity create risks of smuggling, revenue leakage, and opaque external partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou is deepening security ties with Russia as relations with France and several Western partners deteriorate. This may preserve regime autonomy in the short term but increases exposure to opaque security-for-resource arrangements and regional isolation.

frictionVectors.title: RWANDA–DRC SECURITY FRICTION
frictionVectors.details: Burundi’s alignment with Kinshasa and hostility toward Kigali deepen border-security risks and constrain trade. Armed-group activity around eastern Congo continues to pressure Burundi’s sovereignty and finances.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND AID DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-funded infrastructure and prospective nickel development offer growth but leave the state dependent on external capital, technical expertise, and opaque contracting.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND MARITIME COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Mindelo and Praia attract European, American, and Chinese interest as Atlantic logistics and maritime-security nodes. Competition creates leverage for Cabo Verde but raises pressure over port access and strategic alignment.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND FOOD IMPORT EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported fuel, food, and desalination infrastructure limits full economic sovereignty. Climate shocks and shipping disruptions can quickly amplify fiscal and social pressures.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE-CONTRACT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbons, timber, mining, and major transport projects remain shaped by foreign firms and lenders, limiting transparent domestic control over strategic assets. Debt and infrastructure financing increase external bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: ANGLOPHONE AND FAR-NORTH INSECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest and insurgent threats around Lake Chad divert state capacity from resource governance. Cross-border insecurity also threatens key roads, ports, and energy corridors.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY–MINING NEXUS
frictionVectors.details: The government relies heavily on Russian-linked security support while gold and diamond concessions remain politically sensitive. This arrangement can protect regime survival but risks opaque revenue flows and reduced national control.

frictionVectors.title: BORDERLAND FRAGMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups, porous borders, and instability in Sudan and the wider Sahel constrain state access to mineral zones and trade routes. External security actors therefore retain disproportionate influence over territorial governance.

frictionVectors.title: OIL AND PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chad’s fiscal autonomy remains tied to oil production, foreign operators, and the export pipeline through Cameroon. Price volatility and contract asymmetries limit the government’s room to convert resource wealth into broad-based development.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL AND SUDAN SECURITY PRESSURES
frictionVectors.details: Conflict spillover from Sudan and instability around Lake Chad strain borders, humanitarian systems, and military resources. As Western security relationships adjust, N’Djamena is seeking greater strategic flexibility without losing external backing.

frictionVectors.title: French control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, limiting Comoros' effective territorial sovereignty and access to surrounding maritime resources. The dispute continues to shape relations with Paris and regional diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and energy projects rely heavily on foreign aid, Gulf capital, and diaspora remittances. This provides development support but narrows domestic policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-sector competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt remain central to competition among Chinese firms, Western governments, and Gulf-linked investors. Weak oversight and contract disputes continue to limit the state's ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and regional security
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and alleged external support continues to disrupt eastern trade, mining, and infrastructure. Kinshasa's limited territorial control increases dependence on regional and international security actors.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on oil exports, exposing national revenue and policy space to international energy markets and foreign operators. Diversification and domestic value addition remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-finance exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain important in roads, construction, and extractive-linked projects. These ties expand infrastructure access while raising concerns over debt exposure, procurement transparency, and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa sovereignty gap
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is expanding domestic processing and regulatory leverage, but foreign traders and manufacturers still capture much of the cocoa value chain. Climate stress and farmer incomes remain major vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and transport corridors attract French, Chinese, Gulf, and other international capital. Competition supports growth but creates dependence on external finance and concessionary operators.

frictionVectors.title: Base concentration
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti hosts major foreign military facilities, including those operated by the United States, China, France, Japan, and Italy. The arrangement generates revenue and security guarantees but limits strategic autonomy and increases exposure to great-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port infrastructure and transport corridors are central to the economy, with substantial Chinese involvement and debt exposure. Ethiopia's reliance on Djibouti's maritime access strengthens leverage but also concentrates economic risk.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing and Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: Debt service, IMF-linked reforms, and Gulf investment continue to shape Cairo's fiscal choices. The state retains formal control over strategic infrastructure, but financing needs constrain policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile Security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt remains opposed to unilateral Ethiopian operation of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam without a binding water-management agreement. The dispute directly affects agricultural security and national sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature oil fields and limited diversification leave the state dependent on a shrinking resource base and foreign technical partners. Production-sharing arrangements continue to limit fully sovereign control over upstream capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Large state-led projects and gas-processing ambitions rely on external contractors, lenders, and technology providers. Weak transparency increases the risk that infrastructure serves elite rent extraction more than broad-based economic resilience.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Port and Border Competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's Red Sea coastline gives it strategic leverage as Ethiopia seeks maritime access and regional actors compete for ports. Any bilateral access arrangement could materially alter Eritrea's sovereignty and bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining remains a central source of foreign exchange and depends on external capital, equipment, and marketing networks. This provides revenue but exposes the state to reputational, sanctions, and contractual pressure.

frictionVectors.title: South African Economic Gravity
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's trade, logistics, energy, and financial systems remain heavily integrated with South Africa and the wider SACU framework. This supports stability while narrowing independent control over market access and fiscal policy.

frictionVectors.title: Land and Resource Governance
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, forestry, and water-linked investments remain concentrated among politically connected interests and external commercial partners. Unequal access to land and benefits sustains domestic legitimacy pressures around sovereign resource control.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam strengthens Ethiopia's energy sovereignty but remains the central source of friction with Egypt and Sudan. Disagreement over operating rules and drought coordination keeps escalation risks elevated.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, Corridors, and External Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's pursuit of reliable maritime access brings it into competition with Somalia, Eritrea, Djibouti, Gulf states, and Turkey. External financing and security partnerships could improve connectivity while creating new constraints on strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Transition Legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: The post-coup authorities are asserting greater control over oil and mining policy, but delayed or contested political normalization could weaken investor confidence and external legitimacy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Manganese exports remain dependent on rail and port infrastructure involving foreign operators, limiting Gabon's autonomy over value capture and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese Economic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for transport, food supply, and regional access, creating leverage over trade and border management.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Maritime Control
frictionVectors.details: Illegal or poorly regulated fishing by foreign fleets threatens coastal livelihoods and exposes limited national enforcement capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Gold Mining
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining continues to damage water systems, farmland, and state authority while linking local networks to international gold markets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Strategic Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked mining activity and emerging lithium investment offer capital but raise concerns over licensing transparency, environmental safeguards, and domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Infrastructure Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore corridor has drawn major foreign capital and geopolitical competition, while Guinea struggles to secure durable local processing, revenue, and infrastructure benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Political Transition Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The military government uses resource nationalism to reinforce legitimacy, but uncertainty over elections and institutional checks increases sovereign and investment risk.

frictionVectors.title: Political and Security Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Persistent institutional instability limits the state's ability to regulate ports, concessions, and natural resources, leaving space for foreign and illicit networks.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Cashew Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and dependence on externally controlled cashew trading reduce domestic value capture and strain maritime enforcement.

highlights: Ports and energy remain strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and significant Chinese and Gulf-backed infrastructure exposure constrain Nairobi's room to direct transport and energy policy independently.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu Port and transport corridor are intended to diversify regional trade, but security risks and competition with Mombasa complicate Kenya's effort to capture more value from logistics.

highlights: Water sovereignty depends on South Africa

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: South Africa remains the dominant buyer, financier, and infrastructure partner in Lesotho's water-export system, limiting Maseru's leverage over pricing and strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: High-value diamond mines attract foreign capital and provide fiscal benefits, but ownership, market access, and downstream processing remain largely external.

highlights: Port access is a sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign mining concessions dominate export prospects and infrastructure planning, leaving Liberia exposed to commodity cycles and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Freeport of Monrovia security and control
frictionVectors.details: The port is central to Liberia's trade and regional connectivity, while external operators, donors, and security partners retain substantial influence over its modernization.

highlights: Foreign patrons shape security and exports

frictionVectors.title: Competing oil institutions
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest control of fields, terminals, and revenue channels, preventing a unified sovereign strategy for Libya's main resource.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and energy influence
frictionVectors.details: External security actors and commercial partners retain leverage over force protection, maritime access, and energy deals, reducing Libya's autonomy despite its substantial hydrocarbon base.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and cobalt project exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large foreign-backed mining operations generate exports and jobs but leave Madagascar dependent on external capital, technology, and commodity markets, with limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and logistics bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable power and weak transport links increase reliance on foreign lenders and operators, constraining the state's ability to capture more value from mining and agricultural exports.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed exploration for uranium, rare earths and other minerals is expanding, while Malawi's bargaining power remains limited by fiscal distress and weak regulatory capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and fuel dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower disruptions, fuel shortages and reliance on externally financed generation constrain economic sovereignty and expose the country to imported energy costs.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-contract disputes
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking a larger state share of gold revenues and tighter control over foreign operators, generating repeated tensions with major mining companies and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-access relationship
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on Russian-linked security support increases external leverage over strategic decisions, while persistent insurgency limits effective state control across resource-producing regions.

frictionVectors.title: Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas governance
frictionVectors.details: Offshore gas production with Senegal offers new fiscal and diplomatic leverage, but revenue-sharing, local-content and cross-border governance remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of extractive logistics
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rail and port infrastructure remain dependent on foreign capital and operators, limiting Mauritania's ability to capture full value from its mineral exports.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty transition
frictionVectors.details: The future administration and security use of the Chagos Archipelago remain central to Mauritius's sovereignty, maritime-resource claims and relations with the United Kingdom and United States.

frictionVectors.title: Port and digital-infrastructure rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Indian, Chinese and Western interest in Mauritius's ports, logistics and telecommunications creates investment opportunities but also pressure to preserve strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries and infrastructure projects in Western Sahara continue to generate legal and diplomatic challenges, despite expanding international support for Morocco's autonomy proposal.

frictionVectors.title: Water and energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale desalination, renewable-energy and green-hydrogen projects can strengthen sovereignty, but their financing, technology and export links remain significantly foreign-dependent.

highlights: Cabo Delgado remains the sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled LNG Development
frictionVectors.details: Major offshore gas projects remain dependent on international operators, lenders, and security guarantees. Delays limit state revenue and reduce Maputo's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten communities, logistics corridors, and energy infrastructure. Mozambican forces remain reliant on external military assistance, including regional partners.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of New Energy Projects
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital and technology dominate emerging green-hydrogen, oil, and offshore-development plans. Namibia is seeking stronger local-content and revenue-sharing arrangements to preserve policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Logistics and Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, rail, and electricity constraints could limit sovereign control over mineral and energy value chains. Regional corridors remain essential for exports and expose the country to external commercial leverage.

highlights: Resource sovereignty is being recast through the junta

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiations
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is pressing foreign mining interests for greater state participation and revenue, particularly in uranium. The confrontation risks investment delays, legal disputes, and reduced export capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western forces and deepening ties with Russia and Sahel partners have increased strategic autonomy but weakened intelligence, logistics, and counterinsurgency support. Armed groups continue to exploit the resulting security gaps.

highlights: Oil reform meets entrenched extraction networks
Domestic industrial capacity is expanding unevenly

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Contract Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, pipeline vandalism, and opaque contracting continue to erode public revenue and weaken state control of the Niger Delta. Foreign operators remain central to technology, financing, and offshore production.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Transport Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity, congested ports, and weak rail links constrain domestic processing and manufacturing. Large private projects are improving capacity but also increase dependence on concentrated corporate and foreign financing networks.

highlights: State capacity outpaces regional economic depth
Mineral diplomacy is shadowed by Congo tensions

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Minerals Traceability Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's mineral-trading position faces sustained scrutiny over alleged links between regional supply chains and conflict-affected eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Sanctions and due-diligence requirements could constrain export revenues and diplomatic room.

frictionVectors.title: Security Dependence and Regional Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kigali retains significant internal control but depends on external investment, aid, and security partnerships. Its regional influence generates diplomatic friction that can affect access to infrastructure finance and markets.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Exploration Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Exploration remains dependent on foreign capital and technical capacity, while uncertain commercial prospects limit São Tomé and Príncipe's leverage over prospective offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Portugal, China, and other partners compete for influence through aid, connectivity, and maritime cooperation, giving the government options but also creating financing and alignment pressures.

highlights: Oil and gas era begins cautiously

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Operator Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government's push for greater state participation and contract transparency is testing relationships with international oil and gas companies as offshore production expands.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Coastal Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and coastal infrastructure development remain sensitive sovereignty issues, especially where local livelihoods compete with export-oriented resource projects.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies on external partners, including India and other maritime powers, for surveillance and patrol capacity, creating benefits alongside concerns over strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment dominates tourism and major infrastructure, leaving the islands vulnerable to external shocks while limiting domestic control over key economic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Large-Scale Mining Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mining projects remain central to exports and fiscal expectations, but foreign ownership and limited domestic processing constrain sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, road, and mining logistics projects can improve connectivity but may lock the state into opaque concessions or uneven revenue-sharing arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil and Contract Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Prospective offshore hydrocarbons attract foreign operators and competing external sponsors, while weak institutions and unresolved federal jurisdiction complicate transparent resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Red Sea Rivalries
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other powers seek influence through ports, security agreements, and logistics infrastructure, often intersecting with disputes over federal authority and maritime control.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-security competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is balancing Chinese investment, Western critical-minerals initiatives, and domestic beneficiation demands. Competition over platinum-group metals, manganese, and lithium-related supply chains limits Pretoria's room for strategic alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and logistics bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and congested ports continue to weaken sovereign control over industrial supply chains. Private-sector participation and foreign financing are increasingly necessary to stabilize infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence through Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports depend on infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, leaving production and revenue vulnerable to sabotage, bargaining pressure, and external security actors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of oil value chains
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other international firms remain central to production, services, and financing. Weak domestic institutions and conflict reduce the state's ability to convert resource wealth into broad-based sovereign capacity.

highlights: Gold and ports attract rival sponsors

frictionVectors.title: Gold smuggling and external sponsorship
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed networks and foreign-linked traders continue to channel gold revenues outside transparent state institutions. Gulf, Russian-linked, Egyptian, and regional interests deepen the struggle over mining zones and export routes.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and prospective naval or logistics arrangements have become strategic assets in wider Red Sea competition. The conflict limits Khartoum's ability to negotiate infrastructure access from a position of sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking to monetize major offshore gas reserves while retaining greater control over fiscal terms and local benefits. Negotiations with international energy companies remain sensitive to contract stability and domestic-content demands.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Indian, and Western actors are competing for influence around Dar es Salaam and regional transport corridors. The government must prevent infrastructure financing from creating excessive strategic or debt dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Port influence and trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé gives Togo leverage over Sahel-facing commerce but also attracts competing foreign commercial and security interests. Revenue and logistics resilience remain exposed to regional instability and external shipping conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector control
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates remain strategically important, yet production and value addition are constrained by financing, technology, and market access. Foreign commercial participation can expand output while limiting domestic capture of the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give Brussels significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Fiscal stress limits Tunis's bargaining power despite efforts to preserve strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported hydrocarbons and electricity exposes Tunisia to external price and supply shocks. Delays in renewable investment and grid modernization constrain greater energy sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Lake Albert oil dependency
frictionVectors.details: The oil project links Uganda's export future to foreign capital, technology, and the Tanzania export corridor. Environmental, land, and financing disputes continue to test Kampala's control over the resource chain.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure influence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for transport and energy infrastructure. Debt-service demands and project concentration could narrow Uganda's room to negotiate terms.

highlights: Debt restructuring restores room to maneuver

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Western, Chinese, and Gulf-linked investors are competing for copper and cobalt access. Zambia is seeking more processing and local value capture, but capital and technology dependence remains substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Power and corridor bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and reliance on regional transport corridors limit mining expansion and export resilience. Grid rehabilitation and new corridors are vulnerable to financing delays and external conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of lithium value chains
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain prominent in Zimbabwe's lithium sector, while Harare is pushing beneficiation and tighter export rules. Limited domestic finance and processing capacity weaken the government's ability to capture full value.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financing isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions exposure, restricted credit, and arrears raise Zimbabwe's dependence on non-Western investors and commodity-backed arrangements. This reduces policy flexibility and complicates infrastructure renewal.
